stem: A potential living kidney donor asks whether donation-related costs could affect employment and income. Which teaching point should the coordinator include in living donor education?

options.text: Lost wages related to donation might not be reimbursed
All employers are legally required to provide paid leave for every living donor
Living donors never incur any personal travel or child care expenses
Future donor health problems are always covered by the recipient's insurance

explanation.rationale_correct: Living donor education includes indirect financial impacts such as lost wages that might not be reimbursed, along with other potential employment and insurance consequences.

rationale_incorrect.B: References describe potential lost wages and employment impact, not a universal paid-leave guarantee.
rationale_incorrect.C: Personal expenses such as travel and child care are listed among direct donation-related costs donors should understand.
rationale_incorrect.D: Future donor health problems may not be covered by the recipient's insurance and require disclosure.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Living Donation → donor education → item 12 (financial impact) → b.i.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Lost wages related to donation that might not be reimbursed

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → living donor education → item 12 (financial impact: indirect costs/lost wages); PDF p. 341 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Anchor verified against docs/reference/cupples-core-curriculum-2e.pdf p. 341.

stem: During pre-transplant risk counseling, a candidate asks what can happen if a newly transplanted kidney never functions. Which outcome is explicitly included in standard transplantation risk teaching?

options.text: Primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting and retransplantation
Primary nonfunction is impossible after a technically successful implant
Primary nonfunction resolves spontaneously without any relisting consideration
Primary nonfunction affects only cosmetic wound healing without graft consequences

explanation.rationale_correct: Organ failure risk education includes that primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting and retransplantation, distinguishing it from delayed graft function that may require supportive care.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary nonfunction is a recognized early graft failure risk discussed in pre-transplant counseling.
rationale_incorrect.C: Primary nonfunction may necessitate relisting and retransplantation rather than assumed spontaneous recovery.
rationale_incorrect.D: Primary nonfunction threatens graft function and may require retransplantation, not only cosmetic effects.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §6. Risks associated with transplantation → c. Organ failure → i.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Primary nonfunction may require immediate relisting and retransplantation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §6. Risks associated with transplantation → c. Organ failure (primary nonfunction vs delayed graft function); PDF p. 98 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Distinct 010100 angle from cctc-1006 (rejection timing); anchor verified on Cupples p. 98.

stem: A living liver donor is on the surgical unit the evening of donation. Which postoperative monitoring priority aligns with standard living donor nursing education?

options.text: Monitor for bleeding, wound drainage, and evidence of complications
Defer all wound assessment until the two-year follow-up visit
Assume complications cannot occur because donors are prescreened as healthy
Limit pulmonary monitoring because donors do not receive general anesthesia

explanation.rationale_correct: Despite prescreening, living donors can develop postoperative complications; nursing care includes monitoring for bleeding, wound drainage, and other complication signs.

rationale_incorrect.B: Wound inspection and complication monitoring begin in the immediate postoperative period, not only at long-term follow-up.
rationale_incorrect.C: References explicitly note that complications can occur even in prescreened healthy donors.
rationale_incorrect.D: Donors receive general anesthesia and require pulmonary monitoring including oxygen saturation in the immediate postoperative period.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Living Donation → C. Postoperative Nursing Care of the Live Organ Donor → items 6–7
primary_anchor.quote_hint: The living donor must be monitored for bleeding, wound drainage, and evidence of complications

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → postoperative nursing care of live organ donor (complications despite prescreening; bleeding/wound monitoring); PDF p. 351 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Distinct 010300 angle from cctc-1007 (CMS policy); anchor verified on Cupples p. 351.

stem: According to standard organ-specific indications references, simultaneous heart/lung transplantation is indicated for which candidate profile?

options.text: Concurrent end-stage heart and lung disease, or severe fixed pulmonary hypertension
Isolated end-stage renal disease without cardiopulmonary disease
Stable coronary artery disease amenable to percutaneous intervention only
Acute urinary tract infection without structural heart disease

explanation.rationale_correct: Simultaneous heart/lung transplantation is indicated for concurrent end-stage heart and lung disease or severe fixed pulmonary hypertension, including selected congenital cardiac conditions with pulmonary hypertension.

rationale_incorrect.B: Isolated ESRD is an indication for kidney transplantation, not simultaneous heart/lung transplant.
rationale_incorrect.C: Revascularizable coronary disease is managed medically or surgically without necessarily requiring heart/lung transplant.
rationale_incorrect.D: Untreated infection is a contraindication; it is not an indication for heart/lung transplantation.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 1, Organ-specific indications → C. Simultaneous heart/lung transplantation → item 1
primary_anchor.quote_hint: indicated for either patients with concurrent end-stage heart and lung disease or those with severe, fixed pulmonary hypertension

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → C. Simultaneous heart/lung transplantation (indications); PDF p. 39 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).
